etymology.text: From Middle High German du, duo, dū, from Old High German dū (akin to Old Saxon thū and English thou), from Proto-West Germanic *þū, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

funFacts: German has verbs for it: duzen (to say du) and siezen (to say Sie).
Traditionally, switching from Sie to du was sealed with a drink: Brüderschaft trinken.
pitfalls: Using du with a stranger, a shop assistant or an official can sound rude; the older or higher-ranking person usually offers the du.
Verb ending -st: du isst, du trinkst, du bist, du hast.
subtleties: In letters and e-mails du/dich/dir may be capitalized (Du, Dich, Dir) as a sign of respect; both spellings are correct.
Many companies, start-ups and online services address everyone with du; IKEA in Germany famously does.

The verb takes the 3rd person plural form: Sie sind, Sie haben, Sie essen – never *Sie bist.
subtleties: Sie is used for one person and for several people alike.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German sīn, from Old High German sīn, from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, an analogical infinitive within the suppletive paradigm of “to be” built on Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be, exist”); it replaced the older infinitive wesan (*wesaną “to be, remain”), and forms from *beuną (“to be, exist, become”) also enter the paradigm. Cognate with Dutch zijn.

funFacts: The paradigm mixes old roots: ist/sind (like Latin est, sunt), bin/bist (like English be), war/gewesen (from old wesan, like English was).
pitfalls: Feelings of cold, heat or sickness use the dative: Mir ist kalt / Mir ist schlecht. Ich bin kalt means “I am cold-hearted”.
Perfect with sein, not haben, for motion and change of state: Ich bin gefahren / Er ist gewesen.
Imperative: Sei ruhig! (du) – Seid leise! (ihr) – Seien Sie bitte pünktlich! (polite) – seien is the only Sie-imperative that is not the infinitive.
subtleties: sein is also the possessive “his”/“its” (sein Buch) – a different word with the same spelling.

The dative is ihm – the same form as for er: Ich gebe dem Kind Wasser → Ich gebe ihm Wasser.

Mann (noun, capital, double n) ≠ man (pronoun “one”: Man sagt … = people say …).

subtleties: Grammar asks for es (Das Mädchen … es …), but once the girl is known by name people usually say sie.

etymology.text: From Middle High German kint, from Old High German kind, from Proto-West Germanic *kind, from Proto-Germanic *kindą, *kinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth”).

funFacts: English took kindergarten (“children’s garden”) from German – Friedrich Fröbel opened the first one in 1840.
Kind goes back to the root *ǵenh₁- “to give birth”, the same root as Greek γένος (genos) and Latin genus.
pitfalls: Neuter: das Kind, ein Kind, es.
Plural Kinder, dative plural Kindern: mit den Kindern.
subtleties: Kind is “child” at any age when you mean someone’s son or daughter: Meine Kinder sind 30 und 32.
Genitive des Kindes or des Kinds; the old dative dem Kinde survives in set phrases.

etymology.text: From Middle High German persōn, persōne (ultimately from Latin persōna).

funFacts: Latin persona first meant the mask of an actor – hence also English person and personality.
Russian персона (persona) exists too, but is formal or ironic – the everyday Russian word is человек.
pitfalls: Always feminine, even for a man: Er ist eine nette Person – sie (the person) …
Plural Personen; for “people” in general German prefers Leute or Menschen.
subtleties: Person counts heads (Tisch für vier Personen); Mensch stresses the human being (Er ist ein guter Mensch); Leute is plural only.

etymology.text: From Middle High German liute, from Old High German liuti, also liudi, from Proto-West Germanic *liud(i), from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”). Compare Dutch lieden, Old English lēode (“people”), Polish ludzie, Russian люди (ljudi).

funFacts: Leute and Russian люди are cognates; the same root gave Greek ελεύθερος (eléftheros, “free” – “belonging to the people”, not a slave).
pitfalls: Plural only: there is no singular *Leut. One person = eine Person or ein Mensch.
Dative Leuten: mit den Leuten.
subtleties: die Leute often means “people in general”, “they”: Die Leute reden viel.
With a number, Leute is everyday speech (drei Leute); official texts say Personen.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German vriunt, from Old High German friunt, from Proto-West Germanic *friund, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (“lit., the loving one; lover, loved one, friend”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *preyH-. Cognate with Dutch vriend, English friend, Yiddish פֿרײַנד (fraynd), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌹𐌾𐍉𐌽𐌳𐍃 (frijōnds).

funFacts: Freund literally means “the loving one”: it is an old present participle of a verb “to love”, like English friend and Yiddish fraynd.
pitfalls: mein Freund / meine Freundin usually means boyfriend / girlfriend; for “a friend” say ein Freund von mir / eine Freundin von mir.
Feminine: die Freundin (plural Freundinnen); a mixed group is die Freunde.
subtleties: German separates Freund (a real friend) from Bekannter (an acquaintance) more strictly than English “friend”.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vriundinne, from Old High German friuntinna. Analyzable as Freund + -in.

funFacts: The suffix -in is old: Old High German friuntinna already had it.
pitfalls: mein Freund / meine Freundin usually means boyfriend / girlfriend; for “a friend” say ein Freund von mir / eine Freundin von mir.
Plural with double n: die Freundinnen.
subtleties: -in makes the female form of nouns for people: Freund → Freundin, Lehrer → Lehrerin, Student → Studentin. The female form is always feminine (die) and its plural is -innen.

subtleties: A Schüler stays a Schüler until the Abitur (final exam), even at 19.

etymology.text: From Middle High German dër, from Old High German dër, replacing the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa by analogy with the adjective inflection. Cognate with Yiddish דער (der).

funFacts: The German Sesame Street theme song begins with the three articles: “Der, die, das …”.
pitfalls: Learn every noun with its article: the gender is often not predictable (der Kohl, die Gurke, das Radieschen).
die is feminine singular AND every plural; der is masculine nominative AND feminine dative/genitive AND genitive plural.
subtleties: Compounds take the article of their last part: der Kohl → der Blumenkohl; die Zwiebel → die Frühlingszwiebel.
